You are correct. The title is way wrong and at least the first link from the EFF is full inaccurate statements. The OP doesn't seem to even know what the act is. I've read it and it's not what he claims.

It basically puts laws around things we were already technically doing. It allows the US to enter into information sharing agreements with nations that a committee decides are basically "good guys". Countries with strong data protection laws for it's citizens, good human rights records (like not locking up political opponents), a part of the international cyber security organizations, and things like that to share information for a set category of criminal suspects. The president has to approve it before it can happen and he can only approve the committee's selected nations.

The basics are this

  • Companies can't be held liable for complying with law enforcement agencies that follow legal process for seeking the data.
  • This applies to serious crimes committed in the nation that is the pursuant of data.
  • The data request must adhere to local laws. So, if France is seeking data on a US citizen it must be approved by warrant in a US court. If the US wanted data on a Frenchman then we would have to follow their laws on search.
  • It's a bilateral agreement so if they enter the agreement with us they must reciprocate
  • It forbids seeking data in the US on non citizens on the US which may be used as a route to gather information on a US citizen.
  • This is primarily descriptive of what can be do for a nation's citizens residing at home and aboard and doesn't really get into non citizens other than you can't use that non citizen as a conduit to gather information on a citizen.

It's more or less how we were already supposed to be doing but puts a box on it and if anything it codifies what we can actually do because there weren't strict laws on this.
